    #46433. Breaking: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1843 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
    • I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
    • It has been revealed that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

    I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

    It has been revealed that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

    Sources indicate that I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

    My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

    When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

    It has been revealed that strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

    It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

    That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

    Industry observers note that before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

    Sources indicate that llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

    vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's massive batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

    Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

    I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

    It has been revealed that offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

    If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

    Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the major model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

    All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

    I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

    According to recent reports, first version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

    The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

    It has been revealed that I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

    Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

    That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

    Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

    The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization blueprint of #50245 rather than their own option.

    It has been revealed that qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

    The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

    The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

    Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

    Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

    I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

    Industry observers note that most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

    Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

    These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

    That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

    Sources indicate that most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

    It has been revealed that it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

    Recent findings suggest that transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

    Industry observers note that beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

    Sources indicate that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

    Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

    Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

    #46430. ThreadPoolExecutor result(timeout=1) Left 4 Calls Running

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (704 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    ThreadPoolExecutor result(timeout=1) Left 4 Calls Running

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that future.result(timeout=1) raises TimeoutError after one second, but the thread keeps running the call to the end, and future.cancel() returns False because the work already started; if a tool call must really stop, run it in a child process and terminate that process on timeout.
    • This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program.
    • It has been revealed that here is the version that actually stops the work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that future.result(timeout=1) raises TimeoutError after one second, but the thread keeps running the call to the end, and future.cancel() returns False because the work already started; if a tool call must really stop, run it in a child process and terminate that process on timeout. In my test, four agent tool calls that each "timed out" after 1 s all ran their full 5 s, and the next 0.1 s call on the same pool waited 1.10 s for a free thread.

    This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. All numbers come from CPython 3.14.4 on Linux 7.0, and both scripts ran twice with identical output.

    It has been revealed that here is the version that actually stops the work. It is the code I now use for agent tools that wrap slow, uncooperative functions:.

    The rest of this post is why the thread version cannot do this, and what it costs you when you try.

    Yesterday I wrote about subprocess.run(timeout=1) leaving orphans behind. The same question applies one layer up. A lot of agent frameworks run tool functions in a ThreadPoolExecutor so the event loop stays free, then put a timeout on the future. I wanted to know what that timeout actually does.

    Industry observers note that the test is small: a tool that sleeps 5 seconds and records when it finishes, a pool with four workers, and four calls, each awaited with result(timeout=1). Then a fresh 0.1 s call on the same pool, then the asyncio equivalent, asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.to_thread(...), timeout=1).

    Recent findings suggest that every timeout fired on schedule. None of them stopped anything. All four calls finished at 5.0 s and wrote their results into a list nobody was reading. If those calls had been sending emails or writing rows, all four side effects would have happened after the caller had already logged "tool timed out".

    Recent findings suggest that the concurrent.futures docs are honest about this: "If the call is at the moment being executed or finished running and cannot be cancelled then the method will return False." In other words, it removes queued work, nothing else. Python has no supported way to kill a thread. The timeout on result() is a timeout on your wait, not on the work.

    Recent findings suggest that that distinction is easy to miss because the exception type looks like a verdict. TimeoutError reads as "the call was stopped". It means "I stopped waiting".

    The second line is the one that would hurt in production. After four timeouts the pool looked idle from the caller's side, but all four workers were still busy. A 0.1 s call submitted at that point sat in the queue until a worker came free at the 5 s mark and returned after 1.10 s.

    According to recent reports, scale that up. An agent that retries a slow tool a few times can fill the pool with zombie calls, and then every fast tool queues behind them. Nothing errors. Latency just climbs, and the traces show "timeout" on the slow calls and "slow" on the fast ones, which points you at the wrong thing.

    asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.to_thread(tool, 3), timeout=1) raised at 1.00 s, as advertised. The thread kept going. Then asyncio.run() itself did not return until 8.10 s, because on shutdown it waits for the default executor's threads to finish. So the "1 second" timeout turned into a 2 s stall at exit, well after the caller moved on. In a CLI agent that is the "why does it hang after printing the answer" bug.

    The fix at the top swaps the thread for a one-worker process pool. On timeout, leaving the with block calls terminate() on the worker, so the work really ends. Its output, twice:.

    Sources indicate that the price is about 0.15 s of spawn start-up per call and the usual pickling rules for arguments and results. For tools that call slow external code, that is cheap. For tools that are just HTTP requests, a better fix is a real timeout inside the call, such as an httpx timeout or asyncio.timeout around an async client, because cooperative cancellation never leaves a half-done write behind a killed process.

    Industry News: WARN Act and Your Commuter Benefits — What Happens to Transit and Parking After a Layoff Notice

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A WARN notice gives you at least 60 days' warning before a layoff takes effect.
    • Recent findings suggest that this matters right now.
    • It has been revealed that commuter benefits are formally known as qualified transportation fringe benefits under Section 132(f) of the Internal Revenue Code.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A WARN notice gives you at least 60 days' warning before a layoff takes effect. That notice period protects your paycheck and your time to plan. It does not protect one smaller benefit many commuters overlook: the pre-tax money sitting in your transit and parking account. In most intends, that balance disappears on your last day of work.

    Recent findings suggest that this matters right now. Layoff Atlas presently tracks 756 WARN notices covering 61,768 reported workers in the last 90 days, with 6,464 workers scheduled effective the week of November 21, 6,270 the week of November 28, and 9,467 the week of December 26 — the heaviest week on the calendar. These are reported looks, not confirmed job losses, and coverage varies by state. If your name is on one of those lists, check your transit and parking money first.

    It has been revealed that commuter benefits are formally known as qualified transportation fringe benefits under Section 132(f) of the Internal Revenue Code. They cover transit passes, qualified parking near your workplace or a transit station, and vanpool transportation. Your employer lets you pay for them with pre-tax salary deductions, so the money comes out of your gross pay before federal income tax and payroll taxes.

    For 2026, the IRS allows up to $340 a month in tax-free benefits for transit and vanpool costs combined, and a separate $340 a month for qualified parking. Maxing out both means $680 a month flowing through an account that exists only while you are an employee.

    When your employment ends — resign, laid off, or fired — any unused balance in your commuter account is forfeited back to your employer. No refund, no cash-out, no transfer to a fresh employer's proposal.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not your employer's choice. Federal regulations bar a initiative from refunding salary reductions beyond the benefits actually provided, and the IRS confirmed in Information Letter 2019-002 that the rule applies whether the departure was voluntary or involuntary. The tax code only allows these benefits for current employees, so once you are no longer employed the plan cannot provide benefits, reimburse new expenses, or release unused funds.

    According to recent reports, that makes commuter benefits fundamentally different from a health savings account, where the balance belongs to you and travels with you, and from a medical flexible spending account, which can sometimes be continued through COBRA. Commuter benefits cannot be continued through COBRA at all.

    Recent findings suggest that good news: while you remain employed, unused commuter funds do not expire. Unlike a health FSA, which often forces a year-end spend-down, commuter balances roll from month to month and year to year with no spending deadline. Monthly limits still apply to what you can set aside, but there is no cap on how much can accumulate.

    Sources indicate that that is exactly why the balance can grow large enough to matter. Contribute $200 a month, bike or work from home for a few months, and you can quietly build up several hundred dollars — all of it at risk the day employment ends.

    This is where the WARN Act helps, indirectly. During the 60-day notice period you are still an employee, so your commuter benefits keep working until your actual last day — not the day you receive the notice.

    According to recent reports, every initiative has its own details. Before your last day, confirm your current transit and parking balances, your plan's run-out deadline for submitting claims, and whether your employer concerns physical passes or loads a smart card — a loaded card may have its own expiration or monthly spending window even when the account balance rolls over. If your employer subsidizes your pass directly rather than through salary deductions, that subsidy simply ends with employment.

    It has been revealed that commuter benefits are use-it-or-lose-it in the sharpest sense: useful while you are employed, gone the day you are not. A WARN notice does not change the forfeiture rule, but the 60 days it gives you are enough to spend the balance down, stop new deductions, and file outstanding claims. With 6,270 workers due the week of November 28 and 9,467 the week of December 26, that is a check thousands of workers should make this week.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
    • Sources indicate that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
    • In a recent development, the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

    Sources indicate that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

    In a recent development, the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

    IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

    According to recent reports, foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to fresh series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

    It has been revealed that figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

    Recent findings suggest that now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

    Industry observers note that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

    See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

    Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

    It has been revealed that A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

    Industry observers note that figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

    Sources indicate that time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

    Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

    This approach can help teams in four ways:.

    Recent findings suggest that -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

    -Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

    In a recent development, -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

    Sources indicate that -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

    Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

    The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

    Sources indicate that an ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a latest cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

    To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

    Recent findings suggest that when the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

    Recent findings suggest that the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

    Sources indicate that figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

    A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

    It has been revealed that AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each upcoming reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

    It has been revealed that when sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

    According to recent reports, figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

    A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

    With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as newly introduced sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

    Sources indicate that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

    Industry observers note that figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

    Sources indicate that fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

    It has been revealed that A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

    The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

    Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

    Sources indicate that an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

    On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

    If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

    Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

    A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

    It has been revealed that TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

    This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

    Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

    The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

    It has been revealed that figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

    Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

    Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

    In a recent development, airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

    In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

    Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

    #46425. Breaking: Stop Partitioning Disks by Hand: Practical systemd-repart on Linux

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1299 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Stop Partitioning Disks by Hand: Practical systemd-repart on Linux

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every hand-built Linux image eventually grows the same wart: a shell script that pipes commands into sfdisk, calls partprobe, runs resize2fs, and hopes the device really was /dev/sda.
    • Change the disk, add a partition, or boot the same image on a board that enumerates storage differently, and the script either fails halfway or, worse, succeeds against the wrong device.
    • Sources indicate that systemd-repart is the declarative version of that idea.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every hand-built Linux image eventually grows the same wart: a shell script that pipes commands into sfdisk, calls partprobe, runs resize2fs, and hopes the device really was /dev/sda.

    It works exactly once. Change the disk, add a partition, or boot the same image on a board that enumerates storage differently, and the script either fails halfway or, worse, succeeds against the wrong device. The deeper problem is that the script encodes positions. What you actually mean is "this disk should have a swap partition and a root partition that fills the rest.".

    Sources indicate that systemd-repart is the declarative version of that idea. You write small .conf files describing the partitions that should exist, and the tool makes the partition table match. It is incremental by design: existing partitions are matched by type, missing ones are appended, and when the table already matches the configuration it does nothing at all. It is used to build OS images, and it can run from the initrd to adapt a minimal image to whatever disk it landed on.

    This is the practical guide: the mental model, three working configurations, and the failure modes that cost people data.

    Start with the boundaries, because they explain most of the confusing behaviour:.

    Recent findings suggest that if you need to shrink a partition, this is the wrong tool. For creating and growing partitions on an image or a fresh disk, it is the right one.

    Definitions live in *.conf files read from:.

    Industry observers note that files are sorted by filename, ignoring the directory prefix. That sort order is the whole configuration language for "which partition is which", so the numeric prefixes (10-, 20-, 50-) are not cosmetic.

    That has a concrete consequence for A/B root setups: two files with Type=root, named 10-root-a.conf and 20-root-b.conf, will bind to the first and second root partitions respectively. Rename 20-root-b.conf to 05-root-b.conf and you have silently swapped which physical partition each definition controls.

    Industry observers note that newly introduced partitions are not necessarily written in table order on disk. The allocator places each one in the smallest free area large enough to satisfy its constraints, so a late-numbered partition can end up physically before an earlier one. Partition numbers stay stable; offsets do not have to be monotonic.

    Sources indicate that this is where most surprises come from. The allocator takes the free space and distributes it according to three settings:.

    The default is a minimum of 10M and no maximum. That single default explains the most common question: "why did my root partition take the entire disk?" Because you said it could.

    Sources indicate that there is also an automatic floor: with Format= set, the minimum is raised to the minimum size of that filesystem. ESP and XBOOTLDR partitions get bumped to 100M on 512-byte-sector images and 260M on 4K-sector images, even if you asked for less.

    systemd-repart defaults to --dry-run=yes. Running it bare does not write anything; it prints what it would do. That is a good default and a terrible surprise when you think you just resized a disk.

    With no positional argument, the tool operates on the block device backing the root filesystem. Inside the initrd it operates on the device backing /sysroot/ instead. --list-devices shows candidate devices, and passing - as the device makes it print the minimum image size for the configuration without touching anything.

    Recent findings suggest that --pretty=yes gives you a human-readable table plus a graphic of the proposed layout. --json=short or --json=pretty gives machine-readable output, including the verity root hash when relevant.

    The classic first-boot adaptation. On a system where the root partition is the last one and there is unused space after it:.

    Preview against the running disk:.

    Then apply and grow the filesystem:.

    It has been revealed that growFileSystem=yes sets bit 59 of the GPT partition entry flags (the Discoverable Partitions Specification "grow file system" flag). systemd-growfs@.service and the x-systemd.growfs fstab option honour that flag, and systemd-growfs grows a mounted filesystem to the full size of its block device. On partition types that support the flag it defaults to on, so the line is documentation as much as configuration.

    In a recent development, two caveats. First, a partition can only grow into free space immediately after it; if another partition sits behind it, the allocator cannot move things to help. Second, if your root filesystem lives on LVM, md RAID, or another stacked device, there is no GPT "root" partition to match. The packaged unit lists exit code 76 ("can't find the root block device") as a success for exactly this reason.

    Same mechanism, different type. Fixed 4 GiB swap, formatted as swap:.

    Industry observers note that format=swap writes a swap signature; the label is derived from the partition label, which in turn is derived from the partition type when unset. Confirm what you got before wiring it up:.

    Then reference it by label in /etc/fstab:.

    Note that Format= only applies when the partition is newly created. It has no effect on an existing partition, which is why re-running the tool is safe but also why it will never reformat something you already have.

    This is the workflow that replaces image-building shell scripts. Two definitions:.

    Build a minimal image file, populating the root filesystem from a staging directory:.

    According to recent reports, copyFiles= takes source[:target[:options]] and implies Format= if you did not set one (vfat for ESP/XBOOTLDR, ext4 otherwise). Copying stops at filesystem limitations: symlinks, FIFOs, sockets, and device nodes are skipped on vfat with a log message, and UIDs/GIDs are preserved as-is.

    Verify the result without mounting it:.

    Then write it to the target medium with dd or your usual flasher, boot it, and let the on-disk configuration take over.

    Partition UUIDs and the disk UUID are derived by hashing a seed, which by default is the machine ID read from --root=. Images built from the same tree therefore get the same UUIDs. Pass --seed=random when you want them randomized, or an explicit UUID when you need byte-identical rebuilds. This matters for dm-verity and for anything that pins a root hash.

    Encrypt= wraps the partition in LUKS2 before Format= or CopyBlocks= runs, so the filesystem is created inside the encrypted mapping:.

    It has been revealed that encrypt= accepts off, key-file, tpm2, and key-file+tpm2. The LUKS2 UUID is derived from the partition UUID, and the LUKS label defaults to the partition label prefixed with luks- (override with VolumeLabel=, systemd 259+).

    One trap: with Encrypt=key-file and no --key-file=, the empty key is used. That is intentional for provisioning flows where a real passphrase is enrolled later, but it is not what you want on a finished image.

    A partition marked FactoryReset=yes is deleted and recreated empty when the tool runs in factory-reset mode. That mode is triggered by --factory-reset=yes, by systemd.factory_reset=yes on the kernel command line, or by the FactoryResetRequest EFI variable. --can-factory-reset checks whether any partition is marked, exiting zero if so and non-zero otherwise, which is convenient for installer UIs.

    Because it deletes data, treat this as a deliberate feature with a test proposal, not something to enable because it sounds tidy.

    Run these in order the first time you use the tool on real hardware:.

    Recent findings suggest that to restore the table: sudo sfdisk /dev/nvme0n1 < /root/parttable-backup.txt. This restores the partition entries, not filesystem contents, so it is a safety net for table mistakes, not a backup strategy.

    In a recent development, never point --empty=force at a disk you like. It creates a fresh table unconditionally, which in practice means erasing everything.

    For everything else, the payoff is real: the same configuration builds your image, adapts it on first boot, and can be re-run at any time without changing anything. That idempotence is the part shell scripts never quite deliver.

    #46424. Why Learn ML When AI Can Write the Code?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1022 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Learn ML When AI Can Write the Code?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that you can describe a model in plain English and get working code back in seconds.
    • A lot of what used to take a beginner weeks is now nearly free.
    • That changes what's worth memorising.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that you can describe a model in plain English and get working code back in seconds. So it's fair to ask: why spend months learning how machine learning actually works? Because writing the code was never the hard part. The hard part is knowing whether the answer is right, and that part has just become more valuable, not less.

    A lot of what used to take a beginner weeks is now nearly free. Writing a data-cleaning script, wiring up a scikit-learn pipeline, plotting a confusion matrix, drafting a first model: an AI assistant does these in seconds, and usually gets them roughly right.

    That changes what's worth memorising. Nobody needs to recall the exact pandas syntax for a groupby any more. If your strategy for learning ML was "get good at typing the code," that plan really has lost value.

    But notice what AI is producing: an answer. Not a guarantee that the answer is correct for your data, your question, or your business.

    AI tools are very good at producing code that runs. They are much less reliable at telling you whether the result means what you think it means. A model can train without errors, print a good-looking score, and still be useless, because the code was fine and the thinking was flawed.

    Catching that takes a short list of skills that haven't gone anywhere:.

    Sources indicate that each of these rests on concepts: distributions, sampling, bias and variance, leakage, evaluation metrics. You don't get them by prompting. You get them by understanding the ideas well enough to notice when something looks off.

    Recent findings suggest that three situations come up constantly in real data science work. In each one, the model's output is only the starting point, and the decision that matters is made by a person.

    1. Checking the output against what you know about the world. Say a delivery-time model predicts 18 minutes for an order placed during a heavy monsoon downpour, the same as on a clear afternoon. The validation metrics look fine, because most of the training data is dry-weather orders. Anyone who has ordered food in the rain knows the prediction is off. That instinct is a test no metric gives you: does this output agree with how the real world behaves?

    The same check applies to why a model predicts what it does. If a churn model claims the strongest predictor is the number of support tickets, someone who knows the business asks two things. Do tickets cause churn, or do unhappy customers simply file more of them? And would that number even exist at the moment you need the prediction? If it only appears after the customer has already left, the "insight" is leakage, and the great-looking score is the model reading the answer off the page.

    Industry observers note that 2. Deciding what a result lets you conclude. Suppose your regression highlights that customers who received a discount coupon churn more. The code runs, the coefficient is significant, and an AI assistant will cheerfully write "coupons increase churn." But coupons were probably sent to customers who already looked likely to leave, so the model is picking up who was targeted, not what the coupon did.

    Sources indicate that prediction asks "who is likely to churn?" Inference asks "what happens if we change something?" They need different data and different caution. Recognising which question you're really answering, and when you need a proper experiment such as an A/B test instead of more modelling, is a human call.

    3. Choosing the bias-variance trade-off. Every model sits somewhere between too simple (high bias: it misses real patterns) and too flexible (high variance: it memorises noise). An AI assistant can run a hyperparameter search and hand you the setting with the best validation score. But that score is often nearly flat across a range of settings, and choosing within the range is a judgment call.

    Imagine predicting hospital readmissions from 2,000 patient records. A deep gradient-boosted model beats a shallow decision tree by a small margin in cross-validation. Which do you ship? The score doesn't contain the answer. It depends on how small the dataset is (a half-point gain on 2,000 rows may just be noise), how much the patient population will shift next year, whether doctors need to understand and trust the reasons behind each prediction, and what each mistake costs. Missing a high-risk patient is worse than an unnecessary check-up, so you may deliberately favour the model that catches more of them, even at a lower overall score. Those are priorities, and the numbers can't set them for you.

    In each case the AI did what it was asked. The failure, or the decision, sat in the question, the data or the trade-off, and only someone who understands the concepts can make it.

    The people getting the most out of AI tools aren't the ones who prompt fastest. They treat the assistant like a very quick, very confident junior colleague: excellent for drafts and options, never the last word. Here's a working pattern that holds up.

    Recent findings suggest that you can only question what you can name, so keep learning the ideas themselves, and learn them by changing something and watching what happens. Dragging an outlier around in the free Spread Explorer reveals in seconds how the range jumps while the IQR holds. That kind of feel is what makes you ask an AI tool the right follow-up question. Spend less energy memorising syntax and more on the ideas behind it.

    You don't need a course or a year-long strategy. Pick one concept, spend an hour on it, and test it yourself:.

    Repeat that a few times a week and you'll build the one skill that AI can't lend you: the instinct that states wait, that doesn't look right.

    AI will keep getting better at writing the code. That makes the people who understand what the code is doing more useful, not less. The ability to question a confident answer is the part worth learning, and it's the part that will still matter in five years.

    #46423. IoT and AI Together: How to Turn Device Data into Better Decisions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (458 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    IoT and AI Together: How to Turn Device Data into Better Decisions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Many factories, warehouses and logistics fleets already have sensors.
    • Combining the Internet of Things (IoT) with AI closes that gap.
    • IoT supplies the signal: temperature, vibration, location, energy use, machine status and more, streamed from devices in the field.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Many factories, warehouses and logistics fleets already have sensors. Fewer have a clear way to use what those sensors collect. Dashboards fill up with numbers, and teams still make decisions by instinct. The gap is rarely the hardware. It is the step between raw data and action.

    Combining the Internet of Things (IoT) with AI closes that gap.

    IoT supplies the signal: temperature, vibration, location, energy use, machine status and more, streamed from devices in the field.

    AI supplies the interpretation. It can spot patterns a person would miss, flag unusual readings and predict problems before they happen.

    Recent findings suggest that on their own, sensors tell you what happened. Together with AI, the system can tell you what is likely to happen next and what to do about it.

    In a recent development, practical use cases Predictive maintenance: vibration or temperature trends can warn that a machine is drifting toward failure, so repairs happen on your schedule instead of after a breakdown. Quality control: computer vision on a production line can catch defects that tired human eyes miss. Logistics: location and condition data from vehicles and shipments can drive route and delivery decisions. Energy management: usage patterns can show where power is being wasted. The building blocks of a working system.

    Devices and connectivity. Sensors and gateways that send reliable data, even on poor networks.

    Data pipeline. A way to clean, store and organize readings. Poor data quality is the most common reason these projects stall.

    According to recent reports, models. Anomaly detection, forecasting or vision models, matched to the actual decision you want to improve.

    It has been revealed that edge versus cloud. Some decisions, such as stopping a machine, need to happen locally in milliseconds. Others, such as weekly trend analysis, suit the cloud. Most real systems use both.

    Sources indicate that action layer. Alerts, work orders or automated responses that reach the people who can act.

    Industry observers note that how to avoid a stalled pilot Start from a business question ("Why do we lose hours to unplanned downtime?") rather than a technology. Pilot on one line, one site or one fleet segment. Agree on a measurable outcome before building. Plan for security from day one: device authentication, encrypted data and access control. Make sure the people on the floor trust and understand the output. Conclusion.

    In a recent development, ioT gives you the data, and AI makes it useful. The companies that benefit most don't start with the biggest deployment. They pick one costly problem, prove value quickly, and scale what works.

    #46421. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
    • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
    • GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

    A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

    GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That proposal is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

    Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

    It has been revealed that we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

    Industry observers note that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

    For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

    It has been revealed that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

    This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

    Industry observers note that these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

    To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

    We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

    Two design choices shaped the work:.

    According to recent reports, we compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

    Sources indicate that distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

    Sources indicate that all numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

    No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

    A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That claims nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It demonstrates how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

    In a recent development, linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

    Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

    In a recent development, catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

    Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

    Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

    One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

    Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

    Industry observers note that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

    Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

    Sources indicate that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

    In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can strategy around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

    What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

    Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

    Sources indicate that the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

    Dharma-AI R&D · We Make AI Your Model.

    #46419. Industry News: Your table grew 44 columns after row one: auditing schema drift before it rewrites your backtest

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Your table grew 44 columns after row one: auditing schema drift before it rewrites your backtest

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, A prediction log looks like a stable object.
    • Here is the same table, read honestly.
    • Every one of those facts changes what a WHERE clause means, and none appear in the query you wrote six weeks ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, A prediction log looks like a stable object. You query it, you get numbers, the numbers move when the model changes. That is the story you tell yourself.

    Here is the same table, read honestly. ai_predictions holds 48,737 rows written between 2026-06-21 and 2026-11-21, across 130 columns. Eight of those columns have never held a single value. Forty-four were born after the first row was inserted. Eleven stopped being written before this month began.

    Every one of those facts changes what a WHERE clause means, and none appear in the query you wrote six weeks ago.

    All counts are from production, not an example schema.

    Sources indicate that postgres knows which columns exist. It does not know when each one started carrying data, or whether it still does. That is one pass over the catalog plus one aggregate per column, and you cannot write it as a single static SELECT because a column name cannot be a parameter. Build one statement per column: on 48k rows the sweep takes about 90 seconds.

    Eight dead columns out of 130 is 6.2% of the schema. Four — eu_band, eu_band_hit_baseline, direction_gate, gate_reason — read like a band-based gating feature that was designed, migrated, and never wired up. They document an intention, not behaviour.

    Grouping all 122 written columns by the month of their first non-null value gives the shape of the project rather than the shape of the data. Seventy-eight were present on day one.

    Sources indicate that the 12 that landed in late June are typical: goal_line_direction, training_word_version, opening_assessment, dtl_at. The 13 in August are the second-market block plus the veto experiment. October's two are free-text reasoning fields. Each is a legitimate feature; each also carved a hole. Before the feature existed the column is null, and a null in a column that was not yet born is indistinguishable from a null in a column that was measured and came back empty.

    According to recent reports, that is the whole problem in one sentence. NULL means three different things and Postgres has one symbol for it:.

    Industry observers note that only the third is a bug. The first is your history. If you cannot tell them apart, you cannot audit anything.

    Sources indicate that ah_v5_p_up is the probability output of a v5 scoring pass. Count non-null rows per month:.

    The column was added in July. It became real in October. Between those two facts, 5,536 rows were written and 1 of them carries the v5 value.

    So WHERE ah_v5_p_up IS NOT NULL GROUP BY month returns a table whose first three rows are empty. Not an error, not a warning. An empty result that looks like "v5 had no disagreements in June", when v5 did not exist in June. Anyone reading the output without the row counts beside it will draw the wrong conclusion, and the conclusion will be self-consistent.

    The fix is not a filter, it is a habit: never publish a monthly series without the denominator next to it, and never let a filter quietly reduce the denominator to zero.

    The second failure is worse: the column is present and populated the whole time.

    According to recent reports, ah_tier exists from the first row and holds 46,826 values. It is a small integer severity bucket. Filter ah_tier >= 3 and measure the settlement rate per month:.

    The column is not null in June. The value is simply never 3 or higher. The tier assignment logic that produces 3+ went live in September, so the filter returns zero rows for the first three months and then jumps to a +6.35pp lift.

    Read that as a result and you conclude the tier rule has predictive value. Read it as a schema event and you conclude the tier rule has no June comparison at all — and the +6.35pp is measured against a September baseline that is itself 4.12pp below June's 62.30%. The filtered September slice, 64.53%, is only 2.23pp above the unfiltered June number it is being quietly compared to. Two things changed at once: the population and the pipeline.

    This is the failure mode I care about most, because no invariant catches it. ah_tier is non-null, in range, type-correct — and incomparable across the boundary where its generating rule changed. Only the month × filter cross-tab exposes it.

    According to recent reports, not every later column is a hole. Two of them behave completely differently.

    confidence_calibrated sits at 98–100% fill in every month back to June. That is not plausible for a later addition — the value was recomputed and written back over the whole history. A backfill.

    training_word_version shows a different signature:.

    Nine percent is the fingerprint of a pipeline emitting the field incidentally — some code path that happened to serialize the object. The jump to 92% in August is deliberate adoption. Nothing before August can be segmented by training word version, and no backfill is possible: you cannot reconstruct which word a model carried eight weeks ago if nobody wrote it down.

    Both columns pass a naive count(*) completeness check. Only the monthly breakdown indicates which history is real.

    That gives a usable classification from two queries:.

    hit_veto_ss is the interesting one: 26,731 rows accumulated over two months, then switched off on the last day of October. A dashboard built on it still renders — frozen denominator, flat trend line, forever. Nobody gets an alert because the query does not fail.

    Industry observers note that the defect isn't that the schema changed. It's that the change was invisible at query time. So make it visible.

    Recent findings suggest that call it for every month before you plot it. Here, assert_available(cur, 'ai_predictions', 'ah_v5_p_up', '2026-06') raises on 0/2,735 and the chart never gets built. The failure moves from "a reader interprets a blank as a zero" to "the job crashes at 03:00 naming the column and the month". That is the trade you want.

    A registry makes the same knowledge durable rather than tribal:.

    It has been revealed that populate it from the inventory query and review the diff monthly. A column flipping from forward_only to abandoned is a change worth a ticket; one flipping to never_used after six months should be dropped from the schema instead of confusing the next reader.

    Three numbers, same database, same day: 130 columns declared, 122 ever written; 44 with no history before their birth date; 11 that stopped before this month began.

    According to recent reports, none of these are data-quality problems in the sense of wrong values. Every value that exists is correct. The defect is temporal: the shape of the record changed while the analyses kept treating it as one continuous population.

    If you take one thing: NULL is not a value, it is a timestamp. Before you group by it, ask when that column started, when it stopped, and whether the WHERE clause you inherited is filtering rows — or filtering history.

    Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+.

    #46418. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (831 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
    • According to recent reports, the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
    • In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

    The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

    According to recent reports, the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

    In a recent development, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

    After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

    The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

    Industry observers note that daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

    Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

    Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

    In a recent development, we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

    We selected tasks using three criteria:.

    RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

    57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

    2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

    Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

    Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

    Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

    Industry observers note that our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

    The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

    Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

    Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

    Sources indicate that we’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

    According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.
